reference.source: Mann's Surgery of the Foot and Ankle
clinicalPearls: The os trigonum is an unfused accessory ossicle behind the talus that, when present, can be compressed in extreme plantarflexion to cause posterior ankle impingement
It is a classic cause of posterior ankle pain in ballet dancers and in footballers and other athletes who repeatedly plantarflex the ankle
Pain is felt deep in the posterior ankle, reproduced by forced passive plantarflexion, and eased by dorsiflexion, which unloads the posterior structures
A prominent posterior talar (Stieda) process can produce the same impingement even without a separate ossicle
The flexor hallucis longus tendon runs immediately medial to the ossicle, so associated flexor hallucis longus tendinopathy and pain on great-toe movement are common
Lateral radiographs, ideally in plantarflexion, demonstrate the ossicle or a prominent process, and MRI shows bone oedema and associated flexor hallucis longus tendinopathy or soft-tissue impingement
Distinguish it from Achilles or retrocalcaneal pathology, posterior tibial or peroneal tendon disorders, and talar stress injury

Management is conservative with activity and technique modification, physiotherapy, and image-guided corticosteroid injection, with arthroscopic or open excision of the ossicle reserved for resistant cases
reference.pathophysiology: The os trigonum forms from a separate ossification centre behind the talus that fails to fuse with the posterolateral talar process; when it does fuse it forms a prominent Stieda process. During extreme plantarflexion, as in ballet en pointe or a footballer striking a ball, the ossicle or prominent process is compressed between the posterior tibial margin and the calcaneus, pinching the intervening soft tissues and producing posterior impingement pain. Repetitive forced plantarflexion causes inflammation across the synchondrosis or a stress reaction, and can fracture or displace the ossicle. Because the flexor hallucis longus tendon passes through its fibro-osseous tunnel immediately medial to the ossicle, the same mechanism frequently irritates that tendon, producing coexistent flexor hallucis longus tendinopathy with pain on great-toe flexion and, sometimes, triggering. The result is a syndrome of activity-related deep posterior ankle pain in individuals who load the ankle in plantarflexion.
additionalDifferentials: Flexor hallucis longus tendinopathy or stenosing tenosynovitis
Achilles or retrocalcaneal disorders including insertional tendinopathy and bursitis
Posterior tibial or peroneal tendon pathology
Posterior ankle soft-tissue impingement without an ossicle
additionalInvestigations: Lateral ankle radiographs, including a plantarflexion view, to show the os trigonum or a prominent posterior process
Forced passive plantarflexion test to reproduce posterior impingement pain
MRI to assess bone oedema and associated flexor hallucis longus tendinopathy or soft-tissue impingement
Assessment of great-toe flexion and any triggering to detect flexor hallucis longus involvement
Diagnostic image-guided local anaesthetic injection to confirm the posterior ankle as the pain source
CT in selected cases to characterise the ossicle and exclude a fracture
Ultrasound to evaluate the flexor hallucis longus tendon dynamically
redFlags: Acute severe posterior ankle pain after an injury suggesting a fracture of the ossicle or posterior process
Neurological symptoms suggesting tarsal tunnel involvement of the tibial nerve
Rest or night pain or a destructive lesion suggesting infection or tumour
Progressive locking or triggering of the great toe indicating significant flexor hallucis longus pathology
reference.prognosis: Many athletes improve with a period of activity and technique modification, physiotherapy, and sometimes an image-guided injection, allowing return to sport or dance. When conservative treatment fails, excision of the os trigonum, whether arthroscopic or open, with release of the flexor hallucis longus if involved, reliably relieves symptoms and generally permits return to full activity, with the arthroscopic approach offering quicker recovery.
pitfalls: Overlooking coexistent flexor hallucis longus tendinopathy that will continue to cause symptoms if not addressed
Attributing posterior ankle pain to the Achilles tendon and missing posterior impingement
Assuming an os trigonum seen on imaging is the cause of pain without confirming it clinically or with an injection
Missing a fracture of the ossicle or posterior talar process after an acute injury
Failing to modify the provocative activity or technique, leading to recurrence
references: Mann's Surgery of the Foot and Ankle
management: Activity and technique modification with relative rest from forced plantarflexion as first-line treatment for this posterior ankle impingement
Physiotherapy and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs to settle synovitis and address associated flexor hallucis longus tendinopathy
Image-guided local anaesthetic and corticosteroid injection into the posterior ankle, which both relieves pain and confirms the source
Posterior ankle decompression by arthroscopic or open excision of the os trigonum or prominent Stieda process, with release of the flexor hallucis longus tendon, when conservative measures fail
Structured rehabilitation and graded return to sport or dance after intervention
Referral to a foot and ankle surgeon for refractory or mechanically limiting symptoms

Red flag (acute fracture, tibial nerve symptoms, rest pain or locking toe)?
Escalate: fracture, infection or tumour review with urgent imaging
Plantarflexion radiograph, impingement test, MRI, injection to confirm source
Does injection into the posterior ankle relieve the pain?
Consider Achilles disorder, flexor hallucis longus tenosynovitis or stress injury
Activity and technique modification; relative rest from forced plantarflexion
Physiotherapy and NSAIDs for synovitis and flexor hallucis longus tendinopathy
Image-guided local anaesthetic and corticosteroid injection into the posterior ankle
Excision of os trigonum or Stieda process with flexor hallucis longus release if needed
Structured rehabilitation and graded return to sport or dance
